nameStory: Water chickweed gets its name from its love of wet, soggy places where regular chickweed might struggle to survive. The 'chickweed' part comes from the fact that chickens and other birds absolutely love to munch on plants in this family. It's also called 'giant chickweed' because it towers over its smaller cousins, sometimes reaching over three feet tall!
description: Water chickweed is a sprawling perennial plant that loves getting its feet wet in New England's damp spots. This member of the pink family can grow anywhere from 4 inches to over 3 feet tall, with weak stems that often lean on other plants for support. It produces small white flowers from June through August and has a somewhat scraggly, informal appearance that makes it look right at home in wild, weedy places.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with 5 deeply notched petals that look almost like 10 narrow petals at first glance, giving them a delicate, star-like appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stems are weak and often sprawl or lean against other vegetation, feeling somewhat soft and succulent when you gently squeeze them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are oval-shaped and smooth-edged, feeling slightly thick and fleshy compared to common chickweed's thinner leaves

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Much larger overall than common chickweed, often reaching 1-3 feet in height with a more robust, sprawling appearance

habitat: Look for water chickweed in consistently moist or wet areas throughout New England - along stream banks, in roadside ditches, around pond edges, and in low-lying areas that stay damp. It particularly loves disturbed wet soils and can often be found growing under shrubs or in the partial shade of larger plants where the ground stays soggy.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fresh green shoots in wet areas, with the characteristic opposite leaves becoming visible early in the season.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with white star-like flowers blooming from June through August, making it easy to distinguish from other wet-area weeds.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline but may still show some flowers into early fall, with stems becoming more sprawling and less upright.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the roots in most areas, though in protected spots some stems may persist looking brown and dried.

funFact: Despite being called 'water chickweed,' this plant is actually more closely related to carnations and pinks than to true aquatic plants - its succulent-like stems and leaves are special adaptations that help it thrive in waterlogged soils where most of its carnation cousins would drown!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with common chickweed, but water chickweed is much larger overall and always found in wet places. Memory trick: 'Water chickweed = WET and BIG, common chickweed = dry and tiny.' Also, squeeze the stem gently - water chickweed feels more succulent and thick.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'chickweed' applies to several different plants that chickens enjoy eating, but they're not all closely related. Water chickweed's scientific name 'aquatica' clearly indicates its water-loving nature, helping distinguish it from the more familiar common chickweed that grows in drier locations.
compareHints: Among the chickweeds and stitchworts in New England, water chickweed stands out for its wet habitat preferences and larger size. While common chickweed grows in gardens and lawns, and the various stitchworts prefer meadows and woods, water chickweed is the soggy-soil specialist. Its flowers look similar to other Stellaria species but the plant's robust, sprawling growth in wet areas makes it distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Stellaria relatives in New England, common chickweed is the only one with that telltale single line of hairs on the stem - other chickweeds and stitchworts are either hairless or fuzzy all over.

Lesser stitchwort differs from common chickweed by having much narrower, grass-like leaves instead of oval ones, and deeply notched petals that create a clear star shape rather than chickweed's more rounded appearance.
Among New England's chickweeds and starworts, boreal starwort is distinguished by its four-angled stems and deeply-lobed petals that create pronounced star shapes.
Star chickweed stands out from other chickweeds by preferring woodland habitats over disturbed areas, and having much larger, more showy flowers than its weedy relatives.
Unlike the common chickweed found in gardens and lawns, bog stitchwort is strictly a wetland specialist with much narrower leaves.
Among New England's starworts and chickweeds, long-leaved starwort stands out for its exceptionally narrow, grass-like leaves and preference for consistently wet habitats.
Wood stitchwort differs from its chickweed cousins mainly in its deeper petal notches and preference for consistently moist woodland soils.
Lesser chickweed differs from common chickweed by typically lacking flowers entirely and being much smaller in all dimensions.
